title: XbotGo AI sports tracking camera with handheld remote

product.name: XbotGo AI sports tracking camera with handheld remote
product.category: AI auto-tracking sports camera / motorised pan mount
product.summary: Lime-green soft-touch body with a built-in wide-angle camera, dark grey end caps printed 'XbotGo', a rotating round base and a clamp-style holder on top, plus a separate grey key remote marked 'Xbot'. Only the exterior is shown, so every internal part (boards, cells, motor, chips) is inferred or assumed from the product class. Scale is estimated by assuming the lens bezel is about 40 mm wide; the main unit is taken as roughly 96 x 68 x 147 mm and the remote as 40 x 12 x 86 mm.
product.powerInput: Assumed USB-C, 5 V up to 2 A, charging an internal Li-ion pack; remote assumed to run on a CR2032 coin cell

verifySteps: Photograph the rear, underside and rating label to confirm the charging port, input rating and mounting thread.
Look up the FCC ID on the label for internal photos and the radio types of the camera and remote.
Measure the main unit and the remote with callipers to correct the scale.
Remove the side caps and open the housing; photograph both sides of each board and read the IC markings.
Read the battery pack label for chemistry, voltage and capacity, and measure pack voltage.
Rotate the body on the base by hand and operate the top arm to identify the motorised axes and the arm's function.
Open the remote battery door to confirm the cell type and scan for a BLE advertisement when a key is pressed.
Measure USB input current during charging with an inline meter.
safety: Contains lithium-ion cells (assumed): do not puncture, short or pry against the pack when opening; disconnect the battery first.
The pan motor can start unexpectedly when powered; keep fingers and cables clear of the base gap.
A coin cell in the remote is a swallowing hazard; keep away from children.
Soft-touch skin and adhesive-fixed caps can tear; use plastic tools and gentle heat.

firmware.controller: U1 Remote 2.4 GHz radio SoC (assumed Nordic nRF52832, QFN) on the Remote PCB. The camera's U1 AI vision processor is a L
firmware.summary: This firmware runs on the handheld remote's radio SoC, the only microcontroller in the design; the camera's vision processor runs Linux, so the pan motor, battery LEDs, recording and the front power key (wired to the PMIC) are handled there and not by this code. The remote scans its seven dome keys, debounces them and sends a 4-byte Bluetooth LE notification carrying held keys, one-shot toggle clicks (centre, record, power), a sequence number and coin-cell level. While a direction key is held the report repeats every 100 ms so the camera can stop the motor if reports stop; a key stuck for more than 30 s is dropped. After 20 s without key activity the remote disconnects and enters System OFF, and any key wakes it. Nothing here has been built or run on hardware, and the chip, pins and protocol are assumptions listed below.

pins.note: Internal pull-up, dome shorts to GND; wake source from System OFF.

Remote dome switches (Remote direction keys: Right)

pins.note: Internal pull-up; wake source; sent as a one-shot click.

build: The remote has no USB or UART, so bring SWDIO, SWCLK, VDD and GND out to test pads and use a J-Link.
Once per board, flash the Adafruit nRF52832 bootloader, which includes the S132 SoftDevice: nrfjprog --program feather_nrf52832_bootloader.hex --chiperase --reset -f nrf52.
Add the line 'upload_protocol = jlink' to the generated platformio.ini, because the default serial DFU needs a UART the remote does not have.
Power the board from a 3.0 V bench supply while flashing; a CR2032 may sag under the debugger.
test: Power from a bench supply at 3.0 V with a 20 mA current limit, no keys pressed; current should average well under 1 mA while advertising and fall to a few microamps about 20 s later when the remote enters System OFF.
Press any key and check with nRF Connect on a phone that 'Xbot Remote' advertises within about a second; connect and confirm the custom service 7b3e0001-... and the Battery Service are present.

Subscribe to characteristic 7b3e0002-... and hold Left: byte 0 should read 0x04 and repeat about every 100 ms with byte 2 counting up; release and confirm a single report with byte 0 = 0x00. Repeat for Up (0x01), Down (0x02) and Right (0x08).
Tap Record: one report should show byte 1 = 0x40 and the following reports 0x00. Tap Centre and expect 0x10 once.
Tap Power briefly and confirm no click bit appears; hold it for more than 1 s and confirm byte 1 = 0x20 appears exactly once.
Let the remote go to sleep, tap Record very briefly, reconnect quickly and confirm the 0x40 click is still delivered; then repeat but wait more than 3 s before subscribing and confirm it is dropped.
Hold a direction key for more than 30 s and confirm byte 0 clears and the remote later sleeps even with the key still held.
Lower the supply to 2.5 V and then 2.1 V and confirm byte 3 and the Battery Service level fall to roughly 50 % and 10 %.

Only then pair with the camera with the pan base free to rotate: confirm the motor stops within about 300 ms of releasing a key, and also when the remote's cell is pulled out mid-pan (this depends on the camera-side timeout).
assumptions: The camera's U1 AI vision processor is a Linux application processor (Rockchip/Ambarella class) and cannot be targeted from PlatformIO, so this firmware covers only the remote; pan motor drive, encoder, IMU, battery LEDs, charger I2C, microphone and recording belong to the camera's Linux software.
The front button's long-press power on/off is handled by the PMIC and the camera software, since SW1 is wired to the PMIC; nothing in this firmware touches it.
The remote SoC is taken to be a Nordic nRF52832 (the design lists Telink, Nordic or Realtek as candidates); a different chip needs a different SDK.
The board id adafruit_feather_nrf52832 is used because it is the generic nRF52832 Arduino target; Arduino pin numbers equal P0.x on it.
A 32.768 kHz crystal is assumed on P0.00/P0.01, because this board variant selects the crystal as the low-frequency clock; without it the SoftDevice will not start.

The key pins are my choice: Up P0.11, Down P0.12, Left P0.13, Right P0.14, Centre P0.15, Power P0.16, Record P0.27. Each key is a dome to GND with an internal pull-up, wired directly and not as a matrix.
P0.20 and P0.22 (bootloader DFU and factory-reset straps), P0.21 (reset), P0.17 and P0.19 (driven as LEDs by the variant at start-up) and P0.09/P0.10 (NFC) are left unused.

The link is Bluetooth LE with the remote as peripheral and a custom GATT service with one 4-byte notify characteristic (held mask, click mask, sequence, battery percent); the UUIDs and format are invented here and the camera software must match them.
There is no pairing or bonding; the camera is expected to accept only its own remote by address, otherwise anyone nearby could connect to the remote.
The camera must stop the pan motor when no report arrives for about 300 ms or the link drops; the remote supports this with a 100 ms repeat while a key is held but cannot enforce it.
The camera owns the toggle states: Centre and Record are sent as single click events on press, and Power as a click after a 1 s hold to avoid accidental standby.
Up and Down are reported as held keys like Left and Right; whether they tilt or shift a digital crop is the camera's decision.
Timings chosen: 5 ms scan, 20 ms debounce, 30 s stuck-key cutoff, 3 s expiry for undelivered clicks, 20 s idle before System OFF, 15 to 30 ms connection interval, 0 dBm transmit power.
Waking the camera from standby with the remote's power key needs the camera to keep its Bluetooth module scanning in standby.
A key that is jammed down when the remote goes to sleep is disconnected until another key wakes the remote.
Coin-cell level is linear from 2.0 V (0 %) to 3.0 V (100 %), measured on VDD with analogReadVDD() from the Adafruit nRF52 core bundled with the pinned platform.
The remote has no LED, buzzer or other output in the design, so none is driven.

unknowns: Nothing inside is visible: all boards, chips, cells and the motor are inferred or assumed from the exterior and the product class.
Battery configuration (2S 18650, 1S2P or pouch) and capacity; read the rating label or the pack.
Charging port type and location; the back and underside are not shown.
Whether there is a second motorised axis (tilt) or only pan.
Purpose of the top arm: phone clamp, handle or accessory holder.
Whether the pinhole above the front button is a microphone or a status LED.
Remote link technology (BLE, proprietary 2.4 GHz or IR) and its battery type.
Base mounting interface (1/4-inch thread, magnet, quick release).
All dimensions are scaled from an assumed 40 mm lens bezel and may be off by 20 percent or more.
verifySteps: Photograph the rear, underside and rating label to confirm the charging port, input rating and mounting thread.
Look up the FCC ID on the label for internal photos and the radio types of the camera and remote.
Measure the main unit and the remote with callipers to correct the scale.
Remove the side caps and open the housing; photograph both sides of each board and read the IC markings.
Read the battery pack label for chemistry, voltage and capacity, and measure pack voltage.
Rotate the body on the base by hand and operate the top arm to identify the motorised axes and the arm's function.
Open the remote battery door to confirm the cell type and scan for a BLE advertisement when a key is pressed.
Measure USB input current during charging with an inline meter.
safety: Contains lithium-ion cells (assumed): do not puncture, short or pry against the pack when opening; disconnect the battery first.
The pan motor can start unexpectedly when powered; keep fingers and cables clear of the base gap.
A coin cell in the remote is a swallowing hazard; keep away from children.
Soft-touch skin and adhesive-fixed caps can tear; use plastic tools and gentle heat.
